lesson.title: Getting the Most Out: The Maximum Power Transfer Theorem
lesson.summary: For a fixed Thevenin source, load power peaks exactly when the load resistance equals the Thevenin resistance, delivering VTh squared over 4 RTh watts, at only 50 percent efficiency.
lesson.body:
Once a source network has been reduced to its Thevenin equivalent, VTh in series with RTh, a natural question is what load resistance RL extracts the most possible power from it. The Maximum Power Transfer theorem answers this precisely: for a fixed VTh and RTh, power delivered to RL is maximized when RL equals RTh exactly, and the maximum power itself works out to Pmax equals VTh squared divided by (4 times RTh). Note this is a statement about squeezing the most watts out of a fixed source, it is not a statement about efficiency, and those two goals actually point in opposite directions, which is the part most students find counterintuitive at first.

Why does the peak happen exactly at RL equals RTh, rather than at some very large or very small load? The load current is VTh over (RTh plus RL), and load power is that current squared times RL, so power equals VTh squared times RL, divided by (RTh plus RL) squared. When RL is very small compared to RTh, most of the source voltage is wasted driving negligible current through the tiny load, so power is low. When RL is very large compared to RTh, the current is choked down to nearly zero, so power is again low, even though the load voltage is nearly VTh. Somewhere in between, the tradeoff between current and voltage across the load balances out at its peak, and calculus confirms that balance point lands exactly at RL equals RTh.

Reusing the Thevenin equivalent from the Norton equivalent example, VTh equals 12 volts and RTh equals 4 ohms. Maximum power transfer occurs at RL equals 4 ohms, and Pmax equals 12 squared, divided by (4 times 4), which is 144 divided by 16, or 9 watts. This matches the load power computed directly in the Norton equivalent example for that same 4 ohm load, which also came out to 9 watts, confirming the peak from two independent directions.

Compare that against nearby load values to see the peak clearly. At RL equals 12 ohms, power equals (12 over 16) squared times 12, which is 0.75 squared times 12, or 0.5625 times 12, giving 6.75 watts, lower than 9. At RL equals 2 ohms, power equals (12 over 6) squared times 2, which is 2 squared times 2, or 8 watts, also lower than 9, and also lower than the 8 watts obtained at RL equals 8 ohms by the same formula, showing the curve is not symmetric in RL even though the underlying tradeoff between current and voltage is symmetric.

The efficiency caveat is worth stating clearly: at the maximum power point, exactly half of the total power generated is dissipated inside RTh itself, since RTh and RL are equal and carry the same current, so only 50 percent efficiency is achieved right at the peak. A power utility company would never target this operating point, since wasting half of every watt generated is unacceptable at scale, but for signal and communication circuits, where the goal is to extract the strongest possible signal from a fixed, high resistance source rather than to conserve energy, matching RL to RTh is exactly the right design choice.
